title: Parikshit's seven days
hook: a king told he has seven days to live spends them listening: the fear of death runs even in the wise
carry: abhinivesha: even the wise cling to life
tomorrow: an arrow shot in the dark. when does it land?

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bharata and the deer, and your line, raga and dvesha, the pull and the push. Today, the last of the five afflictions.
screen: `RAGA, DVESHA — THE PULL AND THE PUSH.`

segments.voice: King Parikshit, Arjuna's grandson, is out hunting, tired and thirsty. He finds a sage sitting in deep meditation who doesn't answer him. In a flash of anger, the king hangs a dead snake around the sage's shoulders and leaves. The sage's young son hears of it and curses him: in seven days, the serpent Takshaka will bite him, and he will die. Parikshit doesn't fight the curse. He gives his kingdom to his son and sits down on the bank of the Ganga.
screen: `A DEAD SNAKE ON A SAGE.` → `SEVEN DAYS TO LIVE.` → `THE KING SITS BY THE GANGA.`

segments.voice: Sages gather. Parikshit asks them one question: what should a person do who is about to die? Then the young sage Shuka arrives, and for seven days he tells the king the Bhagavata Purana, story after story of God, while the king fasts and listens. Near the end, Shuka tells him, in effect: let go of the thought, I am going to die. That's a creature's thinking. Unlike the body, you weren't born, and you won't be destroyed. This is why many Hindus still hold a Bhagavat saptah, a seven-day reading of the whole text, and why families read scripture and say God's name beside someone near the end. Now Patanjali. Sutra 2.9 names the fifth affliction: abhinivesha, clinging to life. It is svarasa-vahi, flowing by its own momentum, like a river downhill, and established even in the wise. Vidushah api. The classical commentary hears in every creature the same wish: may I not stop being. Even a just-hatched worm shrinks from danger. Notice who Parikshit is: a good king, saved by Krishna before he was born. Wisdom alone doesn't empty the fear, and Patanjali doesn't shame anyone for it; he says the afflictions are undone by tracing them back to their source, and quieted by meditation. Parikshit spent his last days on what doesn't die. Day to day, abhinivesha is rarely about dying. It's the grip on how things were: a house, a role, any small ending. The same grab.
screen: `ONE QUESTION, SEVEN DAYS OF STORIES.` · `LET GO OF 'I AM GOING TO DIE.'` · `2.9: CLINGING, BY ITS OWN MOMENTUM.` · `EVEN IN THE WISE.` · then, large: `THE SAME GRAB, IN SMALL ENDINGS.`

segments.voice: Let the breath run on its own. On each out-breath, say a name silently: Ram, or Krishna, or Om, whichever name you love; if you don't pray, a word like peace. Notice the little pause at the end of the out-breath, and whether something in you hurries to grab the next one. No need to hold it; let each breath come by itself. If anything feels uncomfortable, breathe normally.
Svarasa-vahi, flowing by its own momentum, like a river downhill. Abhinivesha, the clinging to going on, runs by itself this way, and stays even in the wise.
Your line: abhinivesha, even the wise cling to life. Parikshit spent his seven days on what doesn't die. Go gently; see you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 452 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: AN ARROW IN THE DARK. WHEN DOES IT LAND?`

howItsDone: Many Hindu communities hold a Bhagavat saptah, a seven-day recitation of the Bhagavata Purana that remembers the seven days Parikshit listened to Shuka. Near the end of life, families often read scripture and repeat God's name beside the dying person. Students of the Yoga Sutras study abhinivesha with the classical commentary.

fork.setup: Parikshit learns he has seven days left. by sutra 2.9 and his story, what fits?
options: hunt down the sage's son and break the curse.
sit by the Ganga hearing about God: even the wise meet the fear with practice, not denial.
act as if nothing is happening; the wise feel no fear.
fork.reveal: 2.9 says clinging to life is there even in the wise. Parikshit doesn't pretend; he spends the days on what doesn't die.

original.note: Sanskrit abhiniveśa: settling into, clinging; in the Yoga Sutras, the clinging to life.

trapdoor: what you thought: fear of death is about dying.
what it means: a clinging to going on that runs by itself, shows up in every small ending, and stays even in the wise.
what a scholar hears: abhi-ni-√viś, to enter into or settle down in; the commentary on 2.9 uses the fear in a newborn creature as an argument for memory from earlier lives.

chat.meaning: Parikshit, cursed to die in seven days, spent them hearing the Bhagavata from Shuka. Sutra 2.9 says clinging to life is there even in the wise; the seven-day reading is one way Hindus face it.

Parikshit.meaning: Arjuna's grandson, the king who heard the Bhagavata

Shuka.meaning: Vyasa's son, the sage who told Parikshit the Bhagavata

saptah.meaning: a seven-day reading of a sacred text

abhinivesha.meaning: clinging to life, the wish to go on

svarasa-vahi.meaning: flowing by its own momentum, like a river downhill

Vyasa.meaning: the classical commentator on the Yoga Sutras

Patanjali.meaning: the sage traditionally credited with the Yoga Sutras

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 1.18–1.19 (Parikshit, the sage and the dead snake; the curse of seven days; he sits fasting by the Ganga; Shuka arrives; 'what should one about to die do?')
Bhagavata Purana 12.5 (Shuka: give up the creature's thought 'I will die'; the self is not born and is not destroyed)
Yoga Sutra 2.9 (abhinivesha: flowing by its own momentum, established even in the wise)
Yoga Bhashya on 2.9 (may I not cease to be; the newborn worm)
Yoga Sutra 2.10–2.11 (afflictions removed by tracing back and by meditation)

notes: Sanskrit of 2.9 as rendered: svarasavahi vidusho 'pi tatha rudho 'bhiniveshah. Confirm the reading and the gloss 'established even in the wise'.
Vyasa's example is a creature 'just born' (often rendered worm, krimi); confirm the word and that the commentary presents it as inference from memory of past deaths.
Etymology given as abhi-ni-√viś (to settle into); confirm with a standard lexicon.
'Some modern readers hear instinct there' is a general framing, not a claim about a named scholar.
Review softened 'the one affliction that reading cannot dissolve' (an interpretive claim the sutra does not make) to 'a plain reminder that reading alone doesn't dissolve it'.
